description: We are Team CD Band, four Systems Engineering students from Universidad ORT Uruguay in Montevideo. We enjoy turning complex problems into tools people can actually use. By combining our skills in software development, data processing and interface design, our goal with LunaScout is to make lunar landing-site planning faster, clearer and accessible to everyone, from mission planners to curious students.
summary: LunaScout is a web app that helps plan landings near the Moon's south pole by checking the whole landing ellipse, not just one target point. Landers never touch down exactly where they aim, and at the south pole the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so a few hundred meters can separate sunlight from deadly shadow. For any target, date and set of lander limits (battery, communications and slope), LunaScout checks every point inside the ellipse, hour by hour, using real NASA terrain (LRO LOLA) and Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons. It shows a survival probability, how many days the launch can slip, and better landing sites nearby or across the whole region. Within a single 1 km ellipse, the time in sunlight ranged from 0% to 100% depending on where the lander touched down. When a schedule changes, planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds, without specialist tools. We help missions plan for where they will land, not where they aim.
details:
WOULD YOUR LANDER SURVIVE WHERE IT ACTUALLY LANDS?

Not just where you aim it, but where it actually touches down.

Landers never touch down exactly on their target: they land somewhere inside a landing ellipse that can be more than a kilometer wide. Near the Moon's south pole, where water ice makes future missions so attractive, the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so a small hill can cast a shadow kilometers long and even hide the Earth. A few hundred meters can be the difference between a mission powered by sunlight and one that freezes in the dark.

LunaScout is a web app that turns that risk into something you can see and compare in seconds: it checks every point where your lander might touch down and tells you how likely your mission is to survive.

AIM HERE, LAND ANYWHERE INSIDE THE ELLIPSE

Everything happens on one screen, in three steps.

1. Describe your mission

Pick a target by typing coordinates, clicking the map, or choosing a quick pick. Set the landing date, the mission duration, the size of the landing ellipse and your lander's limits: the longest darkness its batteries can survive, the longest gap without direct contact with Earth, the minimum time with Earth in view, and the maximum safe slope.

2. See every point where you might land

LunaScout analyzes every sample point inside the ellipse on real NASA terrain and colors it: green (viable), amber (risky, close to a limit) or red (not viable). The big number is the survival probability: the share of the ellipse where your mission would survive. Within a single 1 km ellipse, the time in sunlight ranged from 0% to 100% depending on the exact touchdown point. That is why planning for a single point is not enough.

3. Understand why, and find a better option

A timeline shows the Sun and the Earth against the local terrain horizon for the whole mission, with the time left until sunset and Earthset. Each check (sunlight, darkness vs. battery, communications, slope) passes or fails against your limits, and every result shows the terrain resolution behind it.

If the launch slips, LunaScout shows how many days the target stays viable. With one click it suggests better targets nearby, or searches the whole region with "Find best sites", which draws a survival heatmap and ranks the best landing areas for your mission.

REAL NASA DATA, HOUR BY HOUR

1. Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA elevation models give heights and slopes at 5 m per pixel on the Mons Mouton site and 20/40 m per pixel around it.

2. Horizon: for each point, we trace 360 directions over the terrain, out to about 100 km, including the Moon's curvature. There is no atmosphere, so there is no refraction.

3. Sun and Earth: their positions come from NASA JPL Horizons, precomputed hourly for 2025–2028 and converted to each point's local sky.

4. Simulation: for every hour of the mission, we check whether the Sun and the Earth are above that point's horizon.

5. Classification: each point is compared with the lander's limits, and the results are combined into the probability for the whole ellipse.

A full analysis takes under half a second on our server.

CHECKED AGAINST NASA'S OWN SHADOWS

We validated LunaScout against independent references. Our terrain shadows agree 95.5–98.0% with the "Terrain Shadows" layer of LROC QuickMap (about 3,000 points per date, 3 dates), and our Sun and Earth positions match direct JPL Horizons queries within 0.0013°.

WHEN THE LAUNCH SLIPS, RE-PLAN IN SECONDS

Mission plans rarely survive contact with the calendar. When a launch slips, LunaScout lets planners re-check a site, or find a new one, in seconds instead of days. It gives science and engineering teams one shared, visual answer to "where can we land, and when?", and it shows educators and the public why the lunar south pole is one of the hardest places to land in the Solar System.

Because on the Moon, landing is only the beginning: LunaScout helps missions plan for where they will land, not where they aim.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most tools answer "is this point lit?". LunaScout answers "what are my chances where I will actually land?" by treating landing uncertainty as part of the plan, combining terrain, Sun, Earth, lander limits and launch delays in a single probability, and then searching the whole region for better options.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We used real data only, with no hidden safety margins. Each result shows the terrain resolution behind it (5 m vs. 20 m), and we state our limits openly: 20 m terrain can miss small craters, the model assumes an upright lander, and there is no thermal model yet. LunaScout is a planning aid, not an operational tool. Next steps: more south-pole regions, relay-satellite coverage and a thermal model.

TECH STACK

Engine: Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj), with precomputed terrain horizons.

API: FastAPI on Google Cloud Run.

Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Chart.js, on Firebase Hosting.

GitHub repository: https://github.com/lauta-r0/lunar-landing--

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for brainstorming, coding and debugging, interface design mockups, documentation and the validation scripts. Our team chose the concept, defined the requirements, made the design decisions, and reviewed and tested every part of the code and every result. All data comes from NASA and partner sources. No images or media in this project are SI-generated: all screenshots are taken from the working app and our validation outputs.
